4.1.1:
Why this matters

Once Analyze has narrowed the suspects, Improve needs to know how much an X affects the Y, so the team can set it to the right level. Correlation is the first step: does a relationship exist, and how strong is it? This domain carries a heavy share of exam questions for its few topics, so it is high-yield.

The big idea

Correlation measures how strongly two continuous variables move together in a straight-line pattern. Always plot a scatterplot first (2.2.4), then put a number on what you see.

The correlation coefficient describes straight-line patterns only. The bottom-right pattern is a strong relationship with r near zero.

Pearson's correlation coefficient, r

r = Σ(X − X̄)(Y − Ȳ) ÷ √[ Σ(X − X̄)² × Σ(Y − Ȳ)² ]

(This formula is on the IASSC reference sheet.) What it means:

  • r ranges from −1 to +1.
  • Sign = direction: positive means Y rises as X rises; negative means Y falls as X rises.
  • Size (ignoring the sign) = strength: values near 1 or −1 mean the points lie close to a straight line; near 0 means no straight-line pattern.

Rough guide to strength (|r|): above 0.8 strong, 0.5 to 0.8 moderate, below 0.5 weak. These cutoffs vary by field.

r = −0.9 is a stronger relationship than r = +0.6. The sign only shows direction.

r² (the coefficient of determination)

Squaring r gives r²: the share of the variation in Y that is explained by the straight-line relationship with X. If r = 0.9, r² = 0.81: 81% of the variation in Y is explained by X. (In regression, this is R², 4.1.2.)

What correlation does not tell you

  1. r near 0 does not mean "no relationship". It means no straight-line relationship. A strong curved (U-shaped) relationship can have r ≈ 0. Always look at the plot.
  2. Correlation is not causation. Ice cream sales and drownings are correlated because both rise in summer: a lurking variable (temperature) drives both. Two things moving together can be a coincidence, a common cause, or causation in either direction. Proving cause needs a controlled experiment or strong process knowledge.
  3. One point can change everything. A single extreme point (an outlier or an influential point) can create a strong correlation from nothing, or destroy a real one. Check the plot for points far from the rest.

Spearman rank correlation

Spearman's rank correlation applies Pearson's formula to the ranks of the data. It measures any monotonic relationship (consistently increasing or decreasing, not necessarily straight) and resists outliers. Use it for non-normal or ordinal data.

Worked example

Load weight (tons) and fuel use (gallons per 100 miles) for 5 trips: (10, 14), (15, 15), (20, 17), (25, 18), (30, 21).

  1. Means: X̄ = 20, Ȳ = 17.
  2. Deviations of X: −10, −5, 0, 5, 10. Deviations of Y: −3, −2, 0, 1, 4.
  3. Σ(X − X̄)(Y − Ȳ) = 30 + 10 + 0 + 5 + 40 = 85.
  4. Σ(X − X̄)² = 100 + 25 + 0 + 25 + 100 = 250. Σ(Y − Ȳ)² = 9 + 4 + 0 + 1 + 16 = 30.
  5. r = 85 ÷ √(250 × 30) = 85 ÷ 86.6 ≈ 0.98: a very strong positive relationship. r² ≈ 0.96.

Heavier loads go with higher fuel use, as expected. Physics supplies the causal explanation here; in less obvious cases, be careful.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Strength is |r|; the sign is direction.
  • r ≈ 0 can hide a curve. Plot first.
  • Correlation does not prove causation.
  • Check for influential points.

Check yourself

  1. Which is stronger: r = −0.75 or r = 0.70?
  2. r = 0.6. What share of Y's variation is explained by X?
  3. A scatterplot shows a clear U shape, and r = 0.05. What do you conclude?
  4. Shipments and late deliveries are highly correlated across months. Does more volume cause lateness?
  5. When would you use Spearman instead of Pearson?
Show answers
  1. r = −0.75 (|−0.75| > 0.70).
  2. r² = 0.36, so 36%.
  3. There is a strong curved relationship that Pearson's r cannot detect; it is not "no relationship".
  4. Not necessarily. It is plausible, but a lurking variable (season, staffing) could drive both; it needs further investigation.
  5. For non-normal or ordinal data, monotonic but non-linear relationships, or data with outliers.

Key takeaways

  • Plot first. r measures straight-line association from −1 to +1.
  • |r| is strength, sign is direction; r² is the share of variation explained.
  • r ≈ 0 does not rule out a curved relationship.
  • Correlation is not causation; watch for lurking variables and influential points.
  • Spearman: rank-based, for monotonic or non-normal data.
4.1.2:
Why this matters

Correlation says variables are related. Regression gives the actual equation, so you can predict Y for any X, and so you know how much to change X to move Y where you want it. That is exactly what Improve needs: "set the X here to get the Y there."

The big idea

Simple linear regression fits the straight line that best describes how Y changes with X:

Ŷ = b₀ + b₁X
  • Ŷ (Y-hat): the predicted value of Y.
  • b₁: the slope, how much Y changes, on average, for a one-unit increase in X.
  • b₀: the intercept, the predicted Y when X = 0.

The IASSC sheet writes the same line as Ŷ = a + bX.

"Best" means least squares: the line that makes the sum of the squared vertical distances from the points to the line as small as possible.

Each red segment is a residual. Least squares picks the line that makes the sum of their squares smallest.

Calculating the slope and intercept

b₁ = Sxy ÷ Sxx = Σ(X − X̄)(Y − Ȳ) ÷ Σ(X − X̄)²
b₀ = Ȳ − b₁X̄

Using the fuel example from 4.1.1: Sxy = 85, Sxx = 250, X̄ = 20, Ȳ = 17.

  1. b₁ = 85 ÷ 250 = 0.34: each extra ton adds 0.34 gallons per 100 miles.
  2. b₀ = 17 − 0.34 × 20 = 10.2.
  3. Equation: Ŷ = 10.2 + 0.34X.

Predict fuel use at 22 tons: Ŷ = 10.2 + 0.34 × 22 = 17.68 gallons per 100 miles.

Interpreting the intercept: at X = 0 tons, predicted fuel is 10.2: roughly an empty truck. Here it makes sense. Often the intercept has no real meaning (X = 0 may be impossible or far outside the data).

Do not extrapolate

The line is only trustworthy within the range of X values in the data (here 10 to 30 tons). Predicting at 60 tons assumes the straight-line relationship continues, which may not be true (different gearing, engine limits). This is called extrapolation, and it is risky.

How good is the fit? R², S and the p-value

R² (R-squared): the share of variation in Y explained by the model.

R² = SS(regression) ÷ SS(total)

For the example, R² = 28.9 ÷ 30 = 0.963: 96.3% of the trip-to-trip variation in fuel use is explained by load weight. "R² = 0.72" means 72% of the variation in Y is explained by the model; the other 28% is unexplained (other X's and noise).

Adjusted R²: R² corrected for the number of predictors. It matters most in multiple regression (4.2.2), where adding useless terms always raises R² but can lower adjusted R².

S (standard error of the regression): the typical size of the residuals, in Y's units. Here S ≈ 0.61 gallons: predictions are typically off by about 0.6 gallons.

p-value for the slope: tests H₀: slope = 0 (X has no linear effect on Y). If p ≤ α, X is a significant predictor. A confidence interval for the slope that contains 0 matches failing to reject H₀ at that α.

The regression ANOVA table

Regression output includes an ANOVA table that splits the total variation:

SourceSSdfMSF
RegressionSSR1 (k in multiple regression)SSR ÷ dfMS_reg ÷ MS_error
Error (residual)SSEn − 2 (n − k − 1)SSE ÷ df
TotalSSTn − 1

For the example: SST = 30, SSR = 28.9, SSE = 1.1; df = 1, 3, 4; MS_reg = 28.9, MS_error = 0.367; F ≈ 78.8, a highly significant model. S = √MS_error ≈ 0.61. Exam questions often give a partly blank table to fill in.

Reading a coefficient table

TermCoefSE CoefTP
Constant10.200.8112.60.001
Weight0.3400.0388.880.003
  • Coef: the estimated b₀ and b₁.
  • SE Coef: the uncertainty of each estimate.
  • T = Coef ÷ SE Coef; P: the p-value for "this coefficient = 0".
  • Below the table: S, R-sq, R-sq(adj), and sometimes R-sq(pred) (how well the model predicts new data).

The sign of r matches the sign of the slope.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Slope = change in Y per one-unit change in X.
  • R² = share of Y's variation explained, not the share of points on the line.
  • Do not extrapolate.
  • Regression df: 1, n − 2, n − 1 (simple); k, n − k − 1, n − 1 (multiple).
  • The slope and intercept formulas are not on the IASSC sheet: know them.

Check yourself

  1. Ŷ = 50 − 2.5X. What is the predicted Y at X = 8? What does −2.5 mean?
  2. Sxy = 120, Sxx = 40, X̄ = 6, Ȳ = 30. Find b₁ and b₀.
  3. SSR = 80, SST = 100. What is R²?
  4. Simple regression with n = 22: what are the error and total df?
  5. The slope's 95% CI is −0.3 to 1.2. Is X significant at α = 0.05?
Show answers
  1. Ŷ = 50 − 20 = 30. Each one-unit increase in X lowers Y by 2.5 on average.
  2. b₁ = 3; b₀ = 30 − 3 × 6 = 12.
  3. 0.80 (80% explained).
  4. Error df = 20; total df = 21.
  5. No: the interval contains 0.

Key takeaways

  • Ŷ = b₀ + b₁X, fitted by least squares; b₁ = Sxy ÷ Sxx; b₀ = Ȳ − b₁X̄.
  • Slope: change in Y per unit of X. Intercept: Y at X = 0 (may be meaningless).
  • R² = SSR ÷ SST; S = typical residual size; slope p-value tests slope = 0.
  • ANOVA df: 1, n − 2, n − 1; F = MS_reg ÷ MS_error.
  • Do not extrapolate beyond the data.
4.1.3:
Why this matters

A regression equation can look excellent (high R², tiny p-values) and still be wrong, because the model's assumptions are violated. Residual plots are how you check. They are also a favorite exam topic: you are shown a plot and asked what is wrong and how to fix it.

The big idea

A residual is what the model got wrong for each point:

e = Y − Ŷ (observed minus predicted)

In the fuel example, at 30 tons the observed value is 21 and the prediction is 10.2 + 0.34 × 30 = 20.4, so the residual is +0.6. All five residuals are 0.4, −0.3, 0, −0.7, 0.6: they sum to zero, as least-squares residuals always do.

If the model is right, the residuals should look like pure random noise. Any pattern in them is information the model missed.

The assumptions behind regression

  1. Linearity: the true relationship is a straight line (or whatever form you fitted).
  2. Independence: residuals do not influence each other (no time-order effects).
  3. Constant variance: residuals spread the same amount everywhere (homoscedasticity).
  4. Normality: residuals are approximately normal (needed for valid p-values and intervals).

Residuals should also center on zero.

The residual plots

Software usually shows a "four-pack":

  1. Normal probability plot of residuals: points should follow the straight line (normality, 2.2.3).
  2. Histogram of residuals: should look roughly bell-shaped and centered at zero.
  3. Residuals vs fitted values: should be a random, even band around zero.
  4. Residuals vs observation order: should show no pattern over time.

Left: what you want. Middle and right: the two most common problems.

Diagnosing patterns

What you seeProblemFix
Random band around zeroNoneModel OK
Funnel (spread grows or shrinks across the fits)Non-constant varianceTransform Y (log, square root, Box-Cox, 4.2.5)
Curve (U-shape or arch)Wrong functional form: relationship is not linearAdd a squared term (4.2.1) or transform X or Y
Pattern vs order (trend, cycles, runs)Dependence or a time effectInvestigate time-related causes; add a time variable; collect data differently
S-shape or curve on the normal plotNon-normal residualsTransform; check for outliers or a missing variable
One extreme pointOutlier or influential pointCheck the data is correct; assess its influence (4.2.4)

Outliers, leverage and influence

  • An outlier has a large residual: its Y is far from the line.
  • A high-leverage point has an unusual X: far from the other X values. It has the potential to pull the line toward itself.
  • An influential point actually changes the fitted line a lot: removing it would change the slope noticeably. High leverage combined with a large residual is the dangerous combination.

Never delete a point just because it is inconvenient. First check if it is a data error; if it is real, it may be telling you something important.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Residual = observed − predicted.
  • Funnel → non-constant variance → transform Y.
  • Curve → missing curvature → add a squared term or transform.
  • Pattern vs order → dependence or a time effect.
  • A high R² does not prove the model is valid.

Check yourself

  1. Observed Y = 48, predicted Ŷ = 45. What is the residual?
  2. Residuals vs fits fan out wider as fitted values increase. What is wrong, and what is the usual fix?
  3. Residuals vs fits form an arch. What does this mean?
  4. Residuals vs order show steadily increasing values. What should you investigate?
  5. What makes a point influential?
Show answers
  1. 48 − 45 = +3.
  2. Non-constant variance; transform Y (for example log or Box-Cox).
  3. The relationship is curved; add a squared term (or transform).
  4. A time-related effect or dependence (drift, wear, learning, seasonal change).
  5. It substantially changes the fitted line, typically a point with high leverage (unusual X) and a large residual.

Key takeaways

  • Residual e = Y − Ŷ; good models leave random residuals centered at zero.
  • Assumptions: linearity, independence, constant variance, normal residuals.
  • Funnel: transform Y. Curve: add a squared term or transform. Order pattern: time effect. Extreme point: check influence and data.
  • Outlier = big residual; leverage = unusual X; influential = changes the line.
